In [[mathematics]], '''quadratic Jordan algebras''' are a generalization of [[Jordan algebra]]s introduced by {{harvs|txt|first=Kevin|last=McCrimmon|authorlink=Kevin McCrimmon|year=1966}}. The fundamental identities of the [[quadratic representation]] of a linear Jordan algebra are used as axioms to define a quadratic Jordan [[algebra over a field]] of arbitrary characteristic. There is a uniform description of finite-dimensional simple quadratic Jordan algebras, independent of characteristic. If 2 is invertible in the field of coefficients, the theory of quadratic Jordan algebras reduces to that of linear Jordan algebras.

==Definition==
A '''quadratic Jordan algebra''' consists of a vector space ''A'' over a field ''K'' with a distinguished element 1 and a quadratic map of ''A'' into the ''K''-endomorphisms of ''A'', ''a'' ↦ ''Q''(''a''), satisfying the conditions:

* {{math|''Q''(1) {{=}} id}};
* {{math|''Q''(''Q''(''a'')''b'') {{=}} ''Q''(''a'')''Q''(''b'')''Q''(''a'')}} ("fundamental identity");
* {{math|''Q''(''a'')''R''(''b'',''a'') {{=}} ''R''(''a'',''b'')''Q''(''a'')}} ("commutation identity"), where {{math|''R''(''a'',''b'')''c'' {{=}} (''Q''(''a'' + ''c'') − ''Q''(''a'') − ''Q''(''c''))''b''.}}

Further, these properties are required to hold under any [[extension of scalars]].<ref name=Rac1>{{harvnb|Racine|1973|p=1}}</ref>

===Elements===
An element ''a'' is '''invertible''' if {{math|''Q''(''a'')}} is invertible and there exists {{math|''b''}} such that {{math|''Q''(''b'')}} is the inverse of {{math|''Q''(''a'')}} and {{math|''Q''(''a'')''b'' {{=}} ''a''}}: such ''b'' is unique and we say that ''b'' is the '''inverse''' of ''a''.  A '''Jordan division algebra''' is one in which every non-zero element is invertible.<ref name=Rac2/>

===Structure===
Let ''B'' be a subspace of ''A''.  Define ''B'' to be a '''quadratic ideal'''<ref name=Jac153>{{harvnb|Jacobson|1968|p=153}}</ref> or an '''inner ideal''' if the image of ''Q''(''b'') is contained in ''B'' for all ''b'' in ''B''; define ''B'' to be an '''outer ideal''' if ''B'' is mapped into itself by every ''Q''(''a'') for all ''a'' in ''A''.  An '''ideal''' of ''A'' is a subspace which is both an inner and an outer ideal.<ref name=Rac1/>  A quadratic Jordan algebra is '''simple''' if it contains no non-trivial ideals.<ref name=Rac2>{{harvnb|Racine|1973|p=2}}</ref>

For given ''b'', the image of ''Q''(''b'') is an inner ideal: we call this the '''principal inner ideal''' on ''b''.<ref name=Rac2/><ref name=Jac154>{{harvnb|Jacobson|1968|p=154}}</ref>

The '''centroid''' Γ of ''A'' is the subset of End<sub>''K''</sub>(''A'') consisting of endomorphisms ''T'' which "commute" with ''Q'' in the sense that for all ''a''
*''T'' ''Q''(''a'') = ''Q''(''a'') ''T'';
*''Q''(''Ta'') = ''Q''(''a'') ''T''<sup>2</sup>.

The centroid of a simple algebra is a field: ''A'' is '''central''' if its centroid is just ''K''.<ref name=Rac3>{{harvnb|Racine|1973|p=3}}</ref>

===Examples===

====Quadratic Jordan algebra from an associative algebra====
If ''A'' is a unital [[associative algebra]] over ''K'' with multiplication × then a quadratic map ''Q'' can be defined from ''A'' to End<sub>''K''</sub>(''A'') by ''Q''(''a'') : ''b''  ↦ ''a'' × ''b'' × ''a''.  This defines a quadratic Jordan algebra structure  on ''A''.  A quadratic Jordan algebra is '''special''' if it is isomorphic to a subalgebra of such an algebra, otherwise '''exceptional'''.<ref name=Rac2/>

====Quadratic Jordan algebra from a quadratic form====
Let ''A'' be a [[vector space]] over ''K'' with a [[quadratic form]] ''q'' and associated [[symmetric bilinear form]] ''q''(''x'',''y'') = ''q''(''x''+''y'') - ''q''(''x'') - ''q''(''y'').  Let ''e'' be a "basepoint" of ''A'', that is, an element with ''q''(''e'') = 1.  Define a linear functional ''T''(''y'') = ''q''(''y'',''e'') and a "reflection" ''y''<sup>&lowast;</sup> = ''T''(''y'')''e'' - ''y''.  For each ''x'' we define ''Q''(''x'') by

:''Q''(''x'') : ''y'' ↦ ''q''(''x'',''y''<sup>&lowast;</sup>)''x'' − ''q''(''x'') ''y''<sup>&lowast;</sup> .

Then ''Q'' defines a quadratic Jordan algebra on ''A''.<ref>{{harvnb|Jacobson|1968|p=35}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Racine|1973|pp=5–6}}</ref>

====Quadratic Jordan algebra from a linear Jordan algebra====
Let ''A'' be a unital Jordan algebra over a field ''K'' of characteristic not equal to 2. For ''a'' in ''A'', let ''L'' denote the left multiplication map in the [[associative enveloping algebra]]

:<math>L(a) : x \mapsto a x \ </math>

and define a ''K''-endomorphism of ''A'', called the '''[[quadratic representation]]''', by

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)=2L(a)^2 -L(a^2).}</math>

Then ''Q'' defines a quadratic Jordan algebra.

==Quadratic Jordan algebra defined by a linear Jordan algebra==
The quadratic identities can be proved in a finite-dimensional Jordan algebra over '''R''' or '''C''' following [[Max Koecher]], who used an invertible element. They are also easy to prove in a Jordan algebra defined by a unital associative algebra (a "special" Jordan algebra) since in that case ''Q''(''a'')''b'' = ''aba''.<ref>
See:
*{{harvnb|Koecher|1999|pp=72–76}}
*{{harvnb|Faraut|Koranyi|1994|pp=32–34}}</ref> They are valid in any Jordan algebra over a field of characteristic not equal to 2. This was conjectured by [[Nathan Jacobson|Jacobson]] and proved in {{harvtxt|Macdonald|1960}}: [[Ian G. Macdonald|Macdonald]] showed that if a polynomial identity in three variables, linear in the third, is valid in any special Jordan algebra, then it holds in all Jordan algebras.<ref>See:
*{{harvnb|Jacobson|1968|pp=40–47,52}}
</ref> In {{harvtxt|Jacobson|1969|pp=19–21}} an [[elementary proof]], due to McCrimmon and Meyberg, is given for Jordan algebras over a field of characteristic not equal to 2.

===Koecher's proof===
Koecher's arguments apply for finite-dimensional Jordan algebras over the real or complex numbers.<ref>See:
*{{harvnb|Koecher|1999}}
*{{harvnb|Faraut|Koranyi|1994|pp=32–35}}</ref>

====Fundamental identity I====
An element ''a'' in ''A'' is called ''invertible'' if it is invertible in '''R'''[''a''] or '''C'''[''a'']. If ''b'' denotes the inverse, then [[power associativity]] of ''a'' shows that ''L''(''a'') and ''L''(''b'') commute.

In fact ''a'' is invertible if and only if ''Q''(''a'') is invertible. In that case

{{quote box|align=left|::<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)^{-1}a=a^{-1},\,\,\, Q(a^{-1})=Q(a)^{-1}.}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Indeed, if ''Q''(''a'') is invertible it carries '''R'''[''a''] onto itself. On the other hand ''Q''(''a'')1 = ''a''<sup>2</sup>, so

:<math>\displaystyle{(Q(a)^{-1} a)a=a Q(a)^{-1} a=L(a)Q(a)^{-1}a=Q(a)^{-1}a^2 =1.}</math>

The Jordan identity

:<math>\displaystyle{[L(a),L(a^2)](b)=0}</math>

can be [[Polarization of an algebraic form|polarized]] by replacing ''a'' by ''a'' + ''tc'' and taking the coefficient of ''t''. Rewriting this as an operator applied to ''c'' yields

:<math>\displaystyle{2L(ab)L(a) + L(a^2)L(b)=2L(a)L(b)L(a) + L(a^2b).}</math>

Taking ''b'' = ''a''<sup>−1</sup> in this polarized Jordan identity yields

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)L(a^{-1})=L(a).}</math>

Replacing ''a'' by its inverse, the relation follows if ''L''(''a'') and ''L''(''a''<sup>−1</sup>) are invertible. If not it holds for ''a'' + ε1 with ε arbitrarily small and hence also in the limit.

{{quote box|align=left|*If ''a'' and ''b'' are invertible then so is ''Q''(''a'')''b'' and it satisfies the inverse identity:

::<math>\displaystyle{(Q(a)b)^{-1}=Q(a^{-1})b^{-1}.}</math>

*The quadratic representation satisfies the following fundamental identity:

::<math>\displaystyle{Q(Q(a)b)=Q(a)Q(b)Q(a).}</math>
}}
{{Clear}}
For ''c'' in ''A'' and ''F''(''a'') a function on ''A'' with values in End ''A'', let
''D''<sub>''c''</sub>''F''(''a'') be the derivative at ''t'' = 0 of ''F''(''a'' + ''tc''). Then

:<math>\displaystyle{c=D_c(Q(a)a^{-1})=2Q(a,c)a^{-1} +Q(a)D_c(a^{-1}),}</math>

where ''Q''(''a'',''b'') if the polarization of ''Q''

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a,c)={1\over 2} (Q(a+c) -Q(a)-Q(c))=L(a)L(c) + L(c)L(a) - L(ac).}</math>

Since ''L''(''a'') commutes with ''L''(''a''<sup>−1</sup>)

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a,c)a^{-1}= (L(a)L(c) + L(c)L(a) - L(ac))a^{-1}=c.}</math>

Hence

:<math>\displaystyle{c=2c +Q(a)D_c(a^{-1}),}</math>

so that

{{quote box|align=left|::<math>\displaystyle{D_c(a^{-1})= - Q(a)^{-1}c.}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Applying ''D''<sub>''c''</sub> to ''L''(''a''<sup>−1</sup>)''Q''(''a'') = ''L''(''a'') and acting on ''b'' = ''c''<sup>−1</sup> yields

:<math>\displaystyle{(Q(a)b)(Q(a^{-1})b^{-1})=1.}</math>

On the other hand ''L''(''Q''(''a'')''b'') is invertible on an open [[dense set]] where ''Q''(''a'')''b'' must also be invertible with

:<math>\displaystyle{(Q(a)b)^{-1}=Q(a^{-1})b^{-1}.}</math>

Taking the derivative ''D''<sub>''c''</sub> in the variable ''b'' in the expression above gives

:<math>\displaystyle{-Q(Q(a)b)^{-1}Q(a)c =-Q(a)^{-1}Q(b)^{-1}c.}</math>

This yields the fundamental identity for a dense set of invertible elements, so it follows in general by continuity. The fundamental identity implies that ''c'' = ''Q''(''a'')''b'' is invertible if ''a'' and ''b'' are invertible and gives a formula for the inverse of ''Q''(''c''). Applying it to ''c'' gives the inverse identity in full generality.

====Commutation identity I====
As shown above, if ''a'' is invertible,

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a,b)a^{-1} =b.}</math>

Taking ''D''<sub>''c''</sub> with ''a'' as the variable gives

:<math>\displaystyle{0=Q(c,b)a^{-1} + Q(a,b)D_c(a^{-1})=Q(c,b)a^{-1} -Q(a,b)Q(a)^{-1}c.}</math>

Replacing ''a'' by ''a''<sup>−1</sup> gives, applying ''Q''(''a'') and using the fundamental identity gives

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)Q(b,c)a= Q(a)Q(a^{-1},b)Q(a)c = \frac{1}{2}Q(a)[Q(a^{-1}+b) -Q(a^{-1}) -Q(b)]Q(a)c = Q(Q(a)b,a)c.}</math>

Hence

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)Q(b,c)a=Q(Q(a)b,a)c.}</math>

Interchanging ''b'' and ''c'' gives

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)Q(b,c)a=Q(a,Q(a)c)b.}</math>

On the other hand {{math|1=''R''(''x'',''y'')}} is defined by {{math|1=''R''(''x'',''y'')''z'' = 2 ''Q''(''x'',''z'')''y''}}, so this implies

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)R(b,a)c=R(a,b)Q(a)c,}</math>

so that for ''a'' invertible and hence by continuity for all ''a''

{{quote box|align=left|
::<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)R(b,a)=R(a,b)Q(a).}</math>
}}
{{Clear}}

===Mccrimmon–Meyberg proof===

====Commutation identity II====
The Jordan identity {{math|1=''a''(''a''<sup>2</sup>''b'') = ''a''<sup>2</sup>(''ab'')}} can be polarized by replacing ''a'' by ''a'' + ''tc'' and taking the coefficient of ''t''. This gives<ref>{{harvnb|Meyberg|1972|pp=66–67}}</ref>

:<math>\displaystyle{c(a^2b) + 2a (ac)b) = a^2(cb) + 2 (ac)(ab).}</math>

In operator notation this implies

{{quote box|align=left|::<math>\displaystyle{[L(a^2),L(c)]+2[L(ac),L(a)]=0.}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Polarizing in ''a'' again gives

:<math>\displaystyle{c((ad)b) + d((ac)b) + a((dc)b)= (cd)(ab)+(da)(cb)+(ac)(db).}</math>

Written as operators acting on ''d'', this gives

:<math>\displaystyle{L(c)L(b)L(a) +L((ac)b) +L(a)L(b)L(c) = L(ab)L(c)+L(cb)L(a) +L(ac)L(b).}</math>
{{Clear}}
Replacing ''c'' by ''b'' and ''b'' by ''a'' gives

{{quote box|align=left|::<math>\displaystyle{L(b)L(a)^2 +L(a(ab))+L(a)^2L(b)=L(a^2)L(b)+2L(ab)L(a).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Also, since the right hand side is symmetric in ''b'' and '''c'', interchanging ''b'' and ''c'' on the left and subtracting , it follows that the commutators [''L''(''b''),L(''c'')] are derivations of the Jordan algebra.

Let

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)=2L(a)^2 - L(a^2).}</math>

Then ''Q''(''a'') commutes with ''L''(''a'') by the Jordan identity.

From the definitions if {{math|1=''Q''(''a'',''b'') = ½ (''Q''(''a'' = ''b'') − ''Q''(''a'') − ''Q''(''b''))}} is the associated symmetric bilinear mapping, then {{math|1=''Q''(''a'',''a'') = ''Q''(''a'')}} and

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a,b)=L(a)L(b)+L(b)L(a)-L(ab).}</math>

Moreover

{{quote box|align=left|:<math>\displaystyle{2Q(ab,a)=L(b)Q(a) +Q(a)L(b).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Indeed

:{{math|1=2''Q''(''ab'',''a'') − ''L''(''b'')''Q''(''a'') − ''Q''(''a'')''L''(''b'') =   2''L''(''ab'')''L''(''a'') + 2''L''(''a'')''L''(''ab'') − 2''L''(''a''(''ab'')) − 2''L''(''a'')<sup>2</sup>''L''(''b'') − 2''L''(''b'')''L''(''a'')<sup>2</sup> + ''L''(''a''<sup>2</sup>)''L''(''b'') + ''L''(''b'')''L''(''a''<sup>2</sup>).}}

By the second and first polarized Jordan identities this implies

:{{math|1=2''Q''(''ab'',''a'') − ''L''(''b'')''Q''(''a'') − ''Q''(''a'')''L''(''b'') = 2[''L''(''a''),''L''(''ab'')] + [''L''(''b''),''L''(''a''<sup>2</sup>)] = 0.}}

The polarized version of {{math|1=[''Q''(''a''),''L''(''a'')] = 0}} is

{{quote box|align=left|::<math>\displaystyle{2[Q(a,b),L(a)]=2[L(b),Q(a)].}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Now with {{math|1=''R''(''a'',''b'') = 2[''L''(''a''),''L''(''b'')] + 2''L''(''ab'')}}, it follows that

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)R(b,a)=2[Q(a)L(b),L(a)] +2Q(a)L(ab)=2[Q(ab,a),L(a)] +2[L(a),L(b)]Q(a)+2Q(a)L(ab).}</math>

So by the last identity with ''ab'' in place of ''b'' this implies the commutation identity:

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)R(b,a)=2[L(a),L(b)]Q(a)+2L(ab)Q(a)=R(a,b)Q(a).}</math>

The identity ''Q''(''a'')''R''(''b'',''a'') = ''R''(''a'',''b'')''Q''(''a'') can be strengthened to

{{quote box|align=left|::<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)R(b,a)=R(a,b)Q(a)=2Q(Q(a)b,a).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Indeed applied to ''c'', the first two terms give

:<math>\displaystyle{2Q(a)Q(b,c)a=2Q(Q(a)c,a)b.}</math>

Switching ''b'' and ''c'' then gives

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)R(b,a)c=2Q(Q(a)b,a)c.}</math>

====Fundamental identity II====
The identity {{math|1=''Q''(''Q''(''a'')''b'') = ''Q''(''a'')''Q''(''b'')''Q''(''a'')}} is proved using the Lie bracket relations<ref>{{harvnb|Meyberg|1972}}</ref>

{{quote box|align=left|
::<math>\displaystyle{[R(a,b),R(c,d)]=R(R(a,b)c,d) - R(c,R(b,a)d).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Indeed the polarization in ''c'' of the identity {{math|1=''Q''(''c'')''L''(''x'') + ''L''(''x'')''Q''(''c'') = 2''Q''(''cx'',''c'')}} gives

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(c,y)L(x) +L(x)Q(c,y) = Q(yx,c) + Q(cx,y).}</math>

Applying both sides to ''d'', this shows that

:<math>\displaystyle{[L(x),R(c,d)]= R(xc,d) - R(c,xd).}</math>

In particular these equations hold for ''x'' = ''ab''. On the other hand if ''T'' = [''L''(''a''),''L''(''b'')] then ''D''(''z'') = ''Tz'' is a derivation of the Jordan algebra, so that

:<math>\displaystyle{[T,R(c,d)] = R(Dc,d) + R(c,Dd).}</math>

The Lie bracket relations follow because ''R''(''a'',''b'') = ''T'' + ''L''(''ab'').

Since the Lie bracket on the left hand side is antisymmetric,

{{quote box|align=left|::<math>\displaystyle{R(R(a,b)c,d) - R(c,R(b,a)d)=- R(R(c,d)a,b) +R(a,R(d,c)b).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
As a consequence

{{quote box|align=left|:<math>\displaystyle{R(y,Q(x)y)=R(y,x)^2 - 2Q(y)Q(x).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Indeed set ''a'' = ''y'', ''b'' = ''x'', ''c'' = ''z'', ''d'' = ''x'' and make both sides act on ''y''.

On the other hand

{{quote box|align=left|::<math>\displaystyle{2Q(Q(a)b)=2R(a,b)Q(Q(a)b,a)-Q(a)R(b,Q(a)b).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Indeed this follows by setting ''x'' = ''Q''(''a'')''b'' in

:<math>\displaystyle{[R(a,b),R(x,y)]a=- R(R(x,y)a,b)a +R(a,R(y,x)b)a.}</math>

Hence, combining these equations with the strengthened commutation identity,

:<math>\displaystyle{2Q(Q(a)b)=2R(a,b)Q(Q(a)b,a)-R(b,a)Q(a)R(a,b) +2Q(a)Q(b)Q(a)=2Q(a)Q(b)Q(a).}</math>

==Linear Jordan algebra defined by a quadratic Jordan algebra==
Let ''A'' be a quadratic Jordan algebra over '''R''' or '''C'''. Following {{harvtxt|Jacobson|1969}}, a linear Jordan algebra structure can be associated with ''A'' such that, if ''L''(''a'') is Jordan multiplication, then the quadratic structure is given by ''Q''(''a'') = 2''L''(''a'')<sup>2</sup> − ''L''(''a''<sup>2</sup>).

Firstly the axiom ''Q''(''a'')''R''(''b'',''a'') = ''R''
(''a'',''b'')''Q''(''a'') can be strengthened to

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)R(b,a)=R(a,b)Q(a)=2Q(Q(a)b,a).}</math>

Indeed applied to ''c'', the first two terms give

:<math>\displaystyle{2Q(a)Q(b,c)a=2Q(Q(a)c,a)b.}</math>

Switching ''b'' and ''c'' then gives

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)R(b,a)c=2Q(Q(a)b,a)c.}</math>

Now let

:<math>\displaystyle{L(a)=\frac{1}{2}R(a,1).}</math>

Replacing ''b'' by ''a'' and ''a'' by 1 in the identity above gives

:<math>\displaystyle{R(a,1)=R(1,a)=2Q(a,1).}</math>

In particular

:<math>\displaystyle{L(a)=Q(a,1),\,\,\,L(1)=Q(1,1)=I.}</math>

If furthermore ''a'' is invertible then

:<math>\displaystyle{R(a,b)=2Q(Q(a)b,a)Q(a)^{-1}= 2Q(a)Q(b,a^{-1}).}</math>

Similarly if '''b'' is invertible

:<math>\displaystyle{R(a,b)= 2Q(a,b^{-1})Q(b).}</math>

The Jordan product is given by

:<math>\displaystyle{a\circ b = L(a)b=\frac{1}{2}R(a,1)b=Q(a,b)1,}</math>

so that

:<math>\displaystyle{a\circ b = b \circ a.}</math>

The formula above shows that 1 is an identity. Defining ''a''<sup>2</sup> by ''a''∘''a'' = ''Q''(''a'')1, the only remaining condition to be verified is the Jordan identity

:<math>\displaystyle{[L(a),L(a^2)]=0.}</math>

In the fundamental identity

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(Q(a)b)= Q(a)Q(b)Q(a),}</math>

Replace ''a'' by ''a'' + ''t'', set ''b'' = 1 and compare the coefficients of ''t''<sup>2</sup> on both sides:

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)=2Q(a,1)^2 - Q(a^2,1)= 2L(a)^2 - L(a^2).}</math>

Setting ''b'' = 1 in the second axiom gives

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)L(a)=L(a)Q(a),}</math>

and therefore ''L''(''a'') must commute with ''L''(''a''<sup>2</sup>).

==Shift identity==
In a unital linear Jordan algebra the '''shift identity''' asserts that

{{quote box|align=left|:<math>\displaystyle{R(Q(a)b,b)=R(a,Q(b)a).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Following {{harvtxt|Meyberg|1972}}, it can be established as a direct consequence of polarized forms of the fundamental identity and the commutation or homotopy identity. It is also a consequence of Macdonald's theorem since it is an operator identity involving only two variables.<ref>See:
*{{harvnb|Meyberg|1972|pp=85–86}}
*{{harvnb|McCrimmon|2004|pp=202–203}}</ref>

For ''a'' in a unital linear Jordan algebra ''A'' the quadratic representation is given by

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a)=2L(a)^2 - L(a^2),}</math>

so the corresponding symmetric bilinear mapping is

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a,b)=L(a)L(b)+L(b)L(a) -L(ab).}</math>

The other operators are given by the formula

:<math>\displaystyle{\frac{1}{2}R(a,b)=L(a)L(b) -L(b)L(a) +L(ab),}</math>

so that

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(a,b)= 2L(a)L(b)-\frac{1}{2}R(a,b).}</math>

The commutation or homotopy identity

:<math>\displaystyle{R(a,b)Q(a)=Q(a)R(b,a)=2Q(Q(a)b,a),}</math>

can be polarized in ''a''. Replacing ''a'' by ''a'' + ''t''1 and taking the coefficient of ''t'' gives

{{quote box|align=left|:<math>\displaystyle{L(b)Q(a)+R(a,b)L(a)=Q(a)L(b) +L(a)R(b,a)=L(Q(a)b) +2Q(ab,a).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
The fundamental identity

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(Q(a)b)=Q(a)Q(b)Q(a)}</math>

can be polarized in ''a''. Replacing ''a'' by ''a'' +''t''1 and taking the coefficients of ''t'' gives (interchanging ''a'' and ''b'')

{{quote box|align=left|:<math>\displaystyle{2Q(ab,a)= Q(a)L(b) + L(b)Q(a).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Combining the two previous displayed identities yields

{{quote box|align=left|:<math>\displaystyle{ L(Q(a)b)+L(b)Q(a)=L(a)R(b,a),\,\,\,\,L(Q(b)a) +Q(b)L(a)= R(b,a)L(b).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
Replacing ''a'' by ''a'' +''t''1 in the fundamental identity and taking the coefficient of ''t''<sup>2</sup> gives

:<math>\displaystyle{2Q(Q(a)b,b)-L(a)Q(b)L(a)= Q(a)Q(b)+Q(b)Q(a) -Q(ab).}</math>

Since the right hand side is symmetric this implies

{{quote box|align=left|:<math>\displaystyle{2Q(Q(a)b,b)-2Q(Q(b)a,a)= L(a)Q(b)L(a) - L(b)Q(a)L(b).}</math>}}
{{Clear}}
These identities can be used to prove the shift identity:

:<math>\displaystyle{R(Q(a)b,b)=R(a,Q(b)a).}</math>

It is equivalent to the identity

:<math>\displaystyle{2L(Q(a)b)L(b)- Q(Q(a)b,b) = 2L(a)L(Q(b)a) -Q(a,Q(b)a).}</math>

By the previous displayed identity this is equivalent to

:<math>\displaystyle{[L(Q(a)b)+L(b)Q(a)]L(b)= L(a)[L(Q(b)a) + Q(b)L(a)].}</math>

On the other hand, the bracketed terms can be simplified by the third displayed identity. It implies that both sides are equal to {{math|1=½ ''L''(''a'')''R''(''b'',''a'')''L''(''b'')}}.

For finite-dimensional unital Jordan algebras, the shift identity can be seen more directly using [[mutation (Jordan algebra)|mutations]].<ref>{{harvnb|Koecher|1999}}</ref> Let ''a'' and ''b'' be invertible, and let
{{math|1=''L''<sub>''b''</sub>(''a'')=''R''(''a'',''b'')}} be the Jordan multiplication in ''A''<sup>''b''</sup>. Then
{{math|1=''Q''(''b'')''L''<sub>''b''</sub>(''a'') = ''L''<sub>''a''</sub>(''b'')''Q''(''b'')}}.  Moreover
{{math|1=''Q''(''b'')''Q''<sub>''b''</sub>(''a'') = ''Q''(''b'')''Q''(''a'')''Q''(''b'') =''Q''<sub>''a''</sub>(''b'')''Q''(''b'')}}.
on the other hand {{math|1=''Q''<sub>''b''</sub>(''a'')=2''L''<sub>''b''</sub>(''a'')<sup>2</sup> − ''L''<sub>''b''</sub>(''a''<sup>2,''b''</sup>)}} and similarly with ''a'' and ''b'' interchanged. Hence

:<math>\displaystyle{L_a(b^{2,a})Q(b) =Q(b)L_b(a^{2,b}).}</math>

Thus

:<math>\displaystyle{R(Q(b)a,a)Q(b)=Q(b)R(Q(a)b,b)=R(b,Q(a)b)Q(b),}</math>

so the shift identity follows by cancelling ''Q''(''b''). A density argument allows the invertibility assumption to be dropped.

==Jordan pairs==
{{see also|Jordan pair}}
A linear unital Jordan algebra gives rise to a quadratic mapping ''Q'' and associated mapping ''R'' satisfying the fundamental identity, the commutation of homotopy identity and the shift identity. A '''Jordan pair''' {{math|1=(''V''<sub>+</sub>,''V''<sub>−</sub>)}} consists of two vector space {{math|1=''V''<sub>±</sub>}} and two quadratic mappings {{math|1=''Q''<sub>±</sub>}} from {{math|1=''V''<sub>±</sub>}} to {{math|1=''V''<sub>∓</sub>}}. These determine bilinear mappings {{math|1=''R''<sub>±</sub>}} from {{math|1=''V''<sub>±</sub> × ''V''<sub>∓</sub>}} to {{math|1=''V''<sub>±</sub>}} by the formula {{math|1=''R''(''a'',''b'')''c'' = 2''Q''(''a'',''c'')''b''}} where {{math|1=2''Q''(''a'',''c'') = ''Q''(''a'' + ''c'') − ''Q''(''a'') − ''Q''(''c'')}}. Omitting ± subscripts, these must satisfy<ref>{{harvnb|Loos|2006}}</ref>

the fundamental identity

:<math>\displaystyle{Q(Q(a)b)=Q(a)Q(b)Q(a),}</math>

the commutation or homotopy identity

:<math>\displaystyle{R(a,b)Q(a)=Q(a)R(b,a)=2Q(Q(a)b,a),}</math>

and the shift identity

:<math>\displaystyle{R(Q(a)b,b)=R(a,Q(b)a).}</math>

A unital Jordan algebra ''A'' defines a Jordan pair by taking ''V''<sub>±</sub> = ''A'' with its quadratic structure maps ''Q'' and ''R''.
